query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor microalloying addition (~1 at%) of zirconium to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will induce the in-situ formation of nanoscale Zr-rich precipitates at the lamellar interfaces, thereby refining the microstructure and improving the alloy’s strength–ductility balance, creep resistance, and corrosion stability under extreme operating conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure that offers good strength and plasticity but does not fully meet the performance requirements under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, and corrosive environments.
generation.intervention: Incorporate approximately 1 atomic percent zirconium during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Evaluate the modified alloy under industrial-relevant conditions including extreme temperature fluctuations, sustained mechanical loading (to assess room-temperature creep), and aggressive corrosive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of nanoscale, Zr-rich precipitates at the lamellar interfaces that result in refined interlamellar spacing.
generation.mechanism: During solidification, zirconium segregates to the lamellar interfaces and promotes the nucleation of stable nanoscale precipitates. These precipitates act as pinning centers, impeding dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding, which in turn enhances creep resistance and stabilizes the microstructure against degradation during thermal cycling and corrosive exposure while maintaining a balanced strength–ductility profile.
generation.predicted_outcome: The zirconium-modified alloy is expected to demonstrate improved creep resistance, enhanced corrosion stability, and a maintained or slightly improved strength–ductility balance relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (strength, ductility, creep rate, and corrosion resistance) of the original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy without zirconium addition.
generation.boundary: These improvements are anticipated if the alloy processing allows effective zirconium segregation and precipitate formation; deviations such as excessive zirconium content or suboptimal heat treatment could lead to the formation of brittle phases, negating the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the performance enhancements is uncertain and may depend on processing conditions and the precise balance between beneficial precipitate formation and the risk of forming deleterious phases.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using identical synthesis and heat treatment protocols: one set of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and one set with a ~1 at% addition of zirconium. Subject both sets to accelerated testing that simulates extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (to evaluate room-temperature creep), and corrosive conditions. Conduct microstructural characterization using TEM/SEM to confirm the formation and distribution of Zr-rich precipitates.
measurements: Creep rate under defined mechanical loads and temperature conditions
Corrosion resistance metrics (e.g., weight loss, electrochemical behavior)
Mechanical properties such as yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility
Lamellar spacing and nanoprecipitate morphology via TEM/SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the zirconium-modified alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in creep resistance and corrosion stability compared to the baseline, or if the strength–ductility balance is adversely affected (e.g., premature embrittlement or formation of deleterious brittle phases), the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Applying a short, well‐controlled post-solidification aging treatment to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will generate a fine distribution of nano-scale precipitates along the lamellar interfaces, which in turn will improve both its strength and creep resistance under extreme conditions.
drafts.material_initial_state: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with a uniform fine lamellar structure and known limitations in strength–ductility balance, creep resistance, and corrosion performance under variable temperatures.
drafts.intervention: A tailored aging heat treatment designed to trigger nano-precipitation without over-coarsening the existing lamellar microstructure.
drafts.conditions: The treatment must be performed within a narrow temperature and time window (e.g., moderately high temperature for a short duration) to avoid over-aging or segregation that might diminish ductility or induce embrittlement. The intervention is applied post-solidification on samples that have achieved the fine lamellar structure.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of uniformly distributed nano-scale precipitates at or near lamellar interfaces.
drafts.mechanism: The nano-precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion—thus enhancing yield strength—and provide pinning effects that slow grain boundary sliding, reducing creep rates at high temperatures. They may also contribute to stabilizing the microstructure against coarsening during thermal cycling, indirectly supporting improved corrosion resistance by reducing microstructural degradation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical properties (an expected relative increase in both yield strength and creep resistance, potentially on the order of 20-30% improvement compared to the untreated alloy) while maintaining a reasonable ductility, as well as improved stability under thermal cycling indicative of enhanced performance for aerospace fastener applications.
drafts.baseline: As-cast or standard processed AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy exhibiting the fine lamellar structure without the additional aging treatment.
drafts.boundary: The effectiveness of this approach hinges on strict control of aging temperature and time. Excessive treatment may lead to overaging or formation of coarse precipitates that could embrittle the alloy, while insufficient treatment may fail to initiate adequate precipitation strengthening.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples with identical initial lamellar structures. Subject one set to the proposed aging heat treatment while keeping the second set as a control. Perform mechanical testing (such as tensile testing and creep experiments) and accelerated thermal cycling and corrosion tests on both sets.
measurements: Yield strength
Ductility (uniform elongation/plastic strain)
Creep rate under defined high-temperature load
Microstructural analysis using TEM/SEM to observe nano-precipitate distribution
Corrosion rates under accelerated conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in both yield strength and creep resistance (and ideally, thermal stability) compared to the untreated control samples, or if the aging treatment results in a reduction in ductility or introduces harmful microstructural degradations, the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (around 1–2 at.%) of niobium to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will induce the formation of coherent nanoprecipitates at the lamellar interfaces, improving strength, ductility, and high‐temperature creep resistance while maintaining corrosion performance.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure
drafts.intervention: Incorporate a minor niobium addition (approximately 1–2 at.%) during alloy synthesis
drafts.conditions: Performance evaluated under cyclic temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (including room-temperature creep), and in corrosive environments relevant to aerospace fastener applications
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of nano-scale, coherent Nb-rich precipitates distributed along lamellar interfaces
drafts.mechanism: The added niobium is expected to segregate to the lamellar interfaces and form stable, coherent precipitates. These precipitates can hinder dislocation motion and stabilize grain boundaries, thereby enhancing both strength and ductility while reducing creep rates at elevated temperatures without compromising corrosion resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical strengths (e.g., increased yield strength and ductility) along with enhanced creep resistance under operating conditions, relative to the original alloy, with performance improvements that might be in the order of 10% or more if the precipitate formation is optimally controlled.
drafts.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy performance with its uniform fine lamellar structure, which meets some but not all industrial benchmarks in strength–ductility balance and creep resistance
drafts.boundary: This improvement is expected only if the Nb addition remains within a narrow composition window; excessive Nb could form continuous or deleterious phases, adversely affecting ductility and corrosion resistance. Additionally, the processing environment must allow for controlled precipitate formation without introducing significant impurities or defects.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize three sets of samples: one baseline with no Nb addition, one with 1 at.% Nb, and one with 2 at.% Nb under identical processing and thermal treatment. Perform detailed microstructural analysis using TEM, XRD, and SEM to identify precipitate formation and distribution. Evaluate mechanical properties through standardized tensile and creep tests under cyclic temperature conditions and assess corrosion behavior in appropriate aggressive environments.
measurements: Yield strength
Ultimate tensile strength
Ductility (elongation to failure)
Creep rate at relevant temperatures
Corrosion rate
Precipitate morphology and distribution via TEM/XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-added alloys do not show statistically significant improvements (e.g., less than approximately 10% improvement) in strength, ductility, and creep resistance compared to the baseline, or if unfavorable Nb-rich phases are observed that degrade corrosion resistance, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of zirconium (~1 at%) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will refine its lamellar microstructure and promote nanoscale, Zr-rich precipitate formation at the phase interfaces, leading to improved creep resistance and corrosion stability under extreme temperature fluctuations while maintaining the alloy’s strength–ductility balance.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure that offers good strength and plasticity but suboptimal performance for high-temperature, long-term, and corrosive service conditions.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a microalloying addition of approximately 1 atomic percent zirconium during the alloy's synthesis.
drafts.conditions: Test under industrial-relevant conditions including extreme temperature fluctuations, sustained mechanical loading (to assess room-temperature creep), and corrosive environments.
drafts.structural_mediator: Refinement of the lamellar spacing and the formation of nanoscale, Zr-rich precipitates or interfacial particles that act as pinning centers.
drafts.mechanism: Zirconium is expected to segregate to the lamellar interfaces during solidification, reducing the interlamellar spacing and facilitating the nucleation of stable, nanoscale precipitates. These precipitates impede dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding, thereby enhancing creep resistance and corrosion stability without compromising ductility and overall strength.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Enhanced creep resistance and improved corrosion behavior under harsh conditions, with the alloy maintaining or slightly improving its strength–ductility balance relative to the unmodified alloy.
drafts.baseline: The performance of the existing AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy in terms of creep rate, corrosion resistance, and mechanical properties under standard testing conditions.
drafts.boundary: The improvement is expected provided that the alloy processing (e.g., casting and heat treatment) permits effective zirconium segregation and precipitate formation; deviations from these conditions or excessive zirconium content might lead to unwanted brittle phases.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and one set with a 1 at% zirconium addition, using identical casting and heat treatment protocols. Subject both sets to accelerated testing regimes that simulate extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (to assess room-temperature creep), and corrosive environments. Microstructural analysis (using TEM/SEM) should monitor lamellar spacing and precipitate formation.
measurements: Creep rate under defined load and temperature
Corrosion resistance metrics (such as weight loss, electrochemical corrosion potential, or current density)
Mechanical properties including yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility
Microstructural characterization for lamellar spacing and precipitate size/distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the zirconium-modified alloy does not show statistically significant improvement in creep resistance and corrosion performance compared to the baseline alloy, or if the strength–ductility balance is degraded beyond acceptable limits, the hypothesis would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A small addition of titanium to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will promote the in-situ formation of finely dispersed Ti-rich nanoprecipitates at the lamellar interfaces, thereby enhancing its strength–ductility balance, creep resistance, and corrosion stability.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with uniform, fine lamellar structure
drafts.intervention: Introduce a microalloying addition of approximately 0.5–1.0 wt% titanium during alloy processing
drafts.conditions: Performance under cyclic thermal loadings (ambient to ~800°C), long-term room-temperature mechanical loading (creep conditions), and an aggressive corrosive environment (e.g., salt spray or chloride-containing solution)
drafts.structural_mediator: Ti-rich nanoprecipitates formed at the lamellar interfaces
drafts.mechanism: Titanium is expected to form stable, nanoscale precipitates that impede dislocation motion and suppress grain-boundary sliding during long-term loading. In addition, these precipitates may stabilize the interlamellar architecture against degradation during thermal cycling, while also retarding corrosive attack at susceptible interfaces.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is predicted to exhibit an improved combination of strength and ductility, reduced room-temperature creep rates, and enhanced corrosion resistance compared to the unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy.
drafts.baseline: The original performance metrics (strength, ductility, creep rate, and corrosion behavior) of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy without titanium addition
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only within a narrow range of titanium additions; excessive Ti may lead to formation of coarse intermetallic phases that could embrittle the alloy. The observed improvements are also limited to the tested thermal and loading conditions and may not extend to all extremes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples with 0, 0.5, and 1.0 wt% Ti additions. Process them under identical conditions and subject the samples to cyclic thermal treatment (ambient to 800°C) and long-term room-temperature creep tests. Additionally, expose the samples to an accelerated corrosion test (such as salt spray exposure). Microstructural examination using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) will verify nanoprecipitate formation.
measurements: Tensile strength and ductility (to assess the strength–ductility balance)
Creep rate under long-term mechanical loading at room temperature
Corrosion rate in the accelerated test environment
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM) to confirm the formation, size, and distribution of Ti-rich precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-added samples fail to show statistically significant improvements in all three areas (strength–ductility balance, creep resistance, and corrosion stability) compared to the baseline alloy, or if undesired coarse or brittle phases are observed in the microstructure, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
